slides.text: The walls of our Montmartre apartment building were so thin I could hear my neighbor in 4B sigh before she even drew her bow across her cello strings. I was a grumpy novelist nursing a broken heart; she was preparing for the Paris Conservatoire audition. For the first month, whenever she hit a flat note in the Bach suites at midnight, I tapped twice on the plaster radiator pipe in complaint.

Instead of stopping, she plucked two playful pizzicato notes back in the exact rhythm of my knock. Soon, the wall between our beds became a telegraph wire. Three taps meant 'Put the kettle on, it’s raining.' A slow, soaring melody in D-major meant she had heard my typewriter stalling and was sending me courage to finish a chapter. I fell in love with a woman I had only ever known through six inches of lath and plaster.

The night before her audition, she was playing the Elgar concerto when a string snapped with a sharp crack—followed by the quiet, unmistakable sound of her crying against the floorboards. I didn't tap the pipe. I walked out into the hallway in my slippers, knocked softly on the door of 4B holding a fresh pot of chamomile tea, and when she opened it with tear-bright eyes, I said, 'Play it for me from the second movement.'
